author: Unknown
title: Torino è contro il riarmo
content:
Ripubblichiamo l’indizione della due giorni del 19-20 settembre 2026 che si terrà a Torino organizzata dall’assemblea cittadina Torino Partigiana

.


Torino è emblematica in quanto città che viene considerata centrale sia dal punto di vista della riconversione bellica sia dell’innovazione tecnologica: la profonda crisi economica, sociale e culturale che vive la nostra città viene mascherata con il mantra della

Torino che cambia e va veloce

. L’aria della campagna elettorale 2027 non farà che acuire questa propaganda atta a ottenere consenso, da una parte e dall’altra dell’arco della politica istituzionale. 


Il governo Meloni continua ad investire nel riarmo seguendo la linea voluta dagli Stati Uniti di Trump e dall’Unione Europea, sottraendo miliardi a sanità, scuola e servizi per la popolazione. Nell’ultimo anno il nostro paese e la nostra città sono stati teatro di forti mobilitazioni contro la guerra, il genocidio e il governo. Dal movimento per la Palestina dell’autunno scorso passando per la mobilitazione contro lo sgombero di Askatasuna e la grande partecipazione referendaria Torino si è dimostrata partigiana e capace di creare movimento dal basso. 


Politicanti e affaristi di gran parte dell’arco politico istituzionale si sfregano le mani di fronte al business della guerra con il progetto dichiarato di trasformare Torino nella città delle armi. Siamo convinti che questa sia la strada più sbagliata per affrontare la crisi che vive la nostra città e vogliamo smascherare la bolla dentro la quale le politiche dell’amministrazione locale – molto attenta agli interessi degli industriali e dei player privati in ambito produttivo ed energetico – vogliono immergerci assumendo il rischio che questa possa scoppiare approfondendo la crisi sociale che già stiamo vivendo. 


Il nostro obiettivo? Essere scomodi, porre una linea di incompatibilità tra

chi è contro il riarmo e chi non lo è

. Proponiamo di approfondire il confronto e il dibattito attorno al tema del riarmo e della guerra partendo da due giorni di ragionamento collettivo e socialità sabato 19 e domenica 20 settembre.

Sabato ci ritroveremo alle 17.30 per il dibattito dal titolo


“Riarmo europeo: chi vuole la guerra in Europa?” con Elena Basile

.

Domenica dalle ore 10 ci troveremo in assemblea per organizzarci insieme e rispondere alla questione: “Torino città del riarmo: come contrapporsi insieme?”

author: Abdurahman Nur
title: After the Ballot: What Democracy Must Mean for Somalia
content:
Somali political life is intensely debated across towns, households, media platforms and diaspora communities. Yet this energy does not consistently produce the power to compel answers, reverse failed policies or remove officials whose conduct has become unacceptable. The distance between participation and political consequence remains one of Somalia’s central democratic problems.


Direct local elections in Puntland and Mogadishu have provided recent precedents, and

Somalia is again moving towards direct national elections.

 The framework for federal elections, however, has yet to be settled between the government and opposition. The debate should not stop at how votes will be cast. It must also ask what power citizens retain after they have cast them.


Somalia’s First Republic combined universal suffrage and competitive elections with legal opposition,

constitutionally protected civil freedoms and a government required to retain the National Assembly’s confidence

.


The 1969 election produced substantial turnover.

77 of the National Assembly’s 123 sitting members were not returned, including eight members of the outgoing cabinet

. The Somali Youth League (SYL), the governing party at the time, won 73 seats, while parties outside it secured 50. Political scientist Ahmed I. Samatar records that, when the new Assembly first met, all but one of the newly elected non-SYL deputies crossed to the governing party.


The formal result stood. Inside Parliament, most of the opposition strength it had created was gone. That is political attenuation: the balance created by voters remained on paper while losing much of its force inside Parliament. In this case, the attenuation occurred between the election and the new Parliament.


The same election also exposed pressure on the institution meant to keep the contest fair. The government asked police commander Mohamed Abshir Muse to place police personnel and vehicles at the disposal of the governing SYL in electorally important areas. Abshir had defended the force’s political neutrality. He refused and submitted his resignation. A temporary compromise placed him on leave until after the election. Tom J. Farer records that, during his absence, a northern commander known for integrity and political neutrality was recalled to Mogadishu, while more compliant officers were reportedly assigned to important electoral districts. Abshir’s resignation was then accepted.


A delegate casts his vote during the electoral process to choose members of the Lower House of the Somali federal Parliament in Baidoa, Somalia on November 25, 2016. UN Photo/ Sabir Olad


The police were responsible for protecting the election — the government asked them to help it win instead. The episode showed how vulnerable institutional neutrality became when it obstructed those already in power.


Somalia’s current political order was shaped by successive ruptures: colonial division, the discrediting of civilian government, military rule, state collapse and fragmented reconstruction. By 1969, civilian government had lost so much public confidence that the military takeover was widely welcomed. After the state collapsed, political reconstruction relied on a different settlement.


Somalia’s

4.5 formula

, a clan based power-sharing system, allocates equal shares of political representation to four major clan families and a collective half-share to minority groups. It helped restore representation, but also established guaranteed shares and gatekeeping roles for elders and political brokers that have proved difficult to dislodge. The arrangement continued to shape political choices as the surrounding context changed. That persistence is a form of political hysteresis. Research by the Somali Dialogue Platform and Somali Public Agenda describes both its contribution to inclusion and its concentration of political selection among a relatively small group of intermediaries.


Direct elections would return the choice of national representatives to citizens, but they would not automatically remove the political arrangements built around the present system. Candidate selection, party formation and coalition bargaining would still determine how much influence citizens retain after voting. Whether representatives remain visible to those who elected them, whether government answers Parliament and whether political decisions are actually carried out would remain separate questions.


The problem also appears after …

author: Mada Masr
title: What’s behind the US sanctions on Banque Misr UAE?
content:
For Egyptian officials, the singling out of Banque Misr UAE in American sanctions was shocking, even if there are multiple rationales through which the move could be read.


The announcement of sanctions that came on Friday was the latest move in America’s new strategy to suffocate Iran. In mid August, United States President Donald Trump let it be known that he was fed up. After months of negotiations with Iran over an end to a war, a war that the US and Israel started, had failed to materialize, it was time to change tactics. 


This time, it wouldn’t be a new naval blockade on an existing naval blockade. It wouldn’t be more military action.

This time, Trump

wrote

 on his social media account, the pain would come in the form of the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.”


Essentially, the plan, dubbed “Economic D-Day,” a reference to the US invasion of Nazi-held France during World War II, would see Washington DC impose secondary sanctions on any country that “allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran.”


Swooping in to take up the messaging of the plan, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began to beat the war drum of economic sanctions. 


“If you insist on doing business with [Iran], then the US Treasury and U.S. government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent

said

 on August 20.

 “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”


The media was awash in speculation. Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are among Iran’s largest trade partners. Would the US really consider sanctioning such key allies?


And then the decisive day came. On Friday, the US treasury

announced

 its first salvo. 


First to be sanctioned was Reza Mohammad Taeedi, the manager of the Iranian commercial bank Bank Melli’s Dubai branch. 


It made sense: an Iranian bank operating in Dubai surely must be part of a shadow banking operation. 


Next was Kameng Trading Limited, a Hong Kong-based exchange company that has allegedly helped launder funds for a sanctioned Iranian exchange house. 


Again, the proximity to China, which is known to have relations with Iran, made the move legible. 


But the last entity included in the sanctions notice was a surprise. The United Arab Emirates branches of Banque Misr, the Egyptian state-owned bank and the second largest in Egypt, holding assets worth US$83 billion, could see its banking access to US financial institutions revoked, the US treasury announced.


Describing the five branches of what is Egypt’s second largest bank, the US treasury note called the bank “a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to US dollars. Treasury estimates that between January 2024 and June 2026, Banque Misr UAE processed approximately $1.8 billion for 103 companies that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks.”


“Banque Misr UAE’s customers include apparent front companies used by Iran’s Ministry of Defense and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to evade US sanctions, as well as to launder money on behalf of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei,” the statement read. 


The US treasury has given Banque Misr 30 days before the sanctions take effect. In the meantime, it is accepting comments from the public, industry experts and financial institutions about the proposed sanction. 


While the reasons are still unknown, the decision did not materialize out of thin air.


Since around 2023, Egypt has faced a new difficult reality. 


A $23 billion deal with Saudi Arabia inked in 2016 had expired, and while the initial deal had been greased with the handover of Tiran and Sanafir islands, Egypt and Saudi relations had taken a turn for much rockier shores. While the deal extended beyond its initial five-year timeframe, by 2023, Saudi Arabia was no longer willing to provide discounted fuel for Egypt at a time when repeated economic crises were wrecking the country and mounting debt repayments loomed, according to an Egyptian state official who spoke to Mada Masr in early 2025.


To address the shortfall, Egypt had to turn to unconventional solutions at a price that could be affordable. And for Egypt, as for many countries in the region, this meant one thing: Iran.


According to the same source, as well as an Egyptian official and an Egyptian political source, since at least May of 2025, Egypt has been securing shipments of petrochemical products …

author: ROAPE
title: Before there is anything to punish: Burkina Faso’s new citizenship question
content:
On July 16, 2026, when addressing the

Forces vives

 in Yagha Province, Burkina Faso’s transitional president Captain Ibrahim Traoré referred to a statistic that seemed to take even him by surprise. “The number of young Burkinabè studying sharia law abroad is already at one thousand,” he said, and is still rising. Speaking in the context of Burkina Faso’s long-running jihadist insurgency, Traoré suggested that religious education abroad is risky because it can expose young Burkinabè to extremist interpretations of Islam beyond the state’s oversight. He then warned the students to return home, and that failure to do so could lead to them losing their Burkinabè citizenship.


The comment was notable for its religious overtones and some outlets, including members of my WhatsApp group chat where a picture of Traoré with the quote was being shared, seemed to celebrate it as a sign of proactive good governance. But I would say the most interesting thing about Traoré’s comments lies elsewhere. The proposed trigger is the decision to study sharia law abroad. In this sense, citizenship is made conditional before any charge of criminal behaviour, affiliation with a banned group, or participation in political violence. Thus, the threshold is now an educational choice. This deserves more attention because it departs from the way in which the deprivation of citizenship has generally been justified elsewhere.


In the past two decades, governments in countries such as France and the United Kingdom have broadened powers to revoke citizenship, in the name of national security. These measures have been subject to ongoing criticism from lawyers, activists, scholars, and civil liberties organisations concerned about due process and unequal citizenship. However, they have tended to be based on claims of certain conducts: the state provides evidence that some alleged act has been committed or shows a relationship with an organisation deemed to be a threat to security.


So, the present controversy revolves around whether those claims suffice to have a person’s citizenship revoked. But Traoré’s proposal is of a different order. The issue is not that these young Burkinabè have committed any offence, or that there is proven affiliation; the issue is their decision to take advantage of a particular form of education abroad. It looks like the concern precedes the specific matter to be investigated. And this raises a very unusual question: can citizenship itself be conditioned on what the state perceives as a person’s future life trajectory?


In the end, what this will augur for the legal code in Burkina Faso remains to be seen. But even as political rhetoric, the speech is a window into how security can migrate into areas that have traditionally escaped its reach.


Timing is also an important factor, because if the speech had been made in isolation, it might have been dismissed as an off-the-cuff intervention made before a local audience. But recent events point to a larger trend. In May 2026, Burkina Faso

suspended the country’s largest student union for three months

 after it publicly criticised the government. Government officials said the organisation was acting in a way that did not match its educational role. The suspension followed a familiar junta script in which political dissent by students was presented as a problem of public disorder. Barely a month later, another measure got far less international attention. Students from Burkina Faso seeking to pursue higher education abroad

will have to get government authorisation first

. So, going abroad to study is now a matter of prior state approval, not a private educational choice.


When taken together, these developments suggest a slow but steady increase in the government’s control over pathways to educational mobility, through the repositioning of study abroad and student unions within the same field of security governance. However, Traoré’s remarks about citizenship extend this one step further by linking the possibility of nationality itself to personal educational decisions.


There is also a regional dimension to take note of. A day after Traore’s address, the Council of Ministers in Mali

announced proposed amendments to its own citizenship law

, expanding the ability of the state to strip people of nationality under certain circumstances. Until now, there is no public evidence that the Burkinabè and Malian initiatives have been coordinated. It is much too early to …

author: Ivan Mayabi
title: Kenya’s Kairos After the #Occupy Churches Protests
content:
In 2024, a wave of youth-led protests in Kenya, which organizers and commentators came to call “Occupy Churches”, directed itself not at the state but at the country’s most visible religious institutions – its megachurches, its prosperity preachers, the whole apparatus of what scholars call the “

neo-Pentecostal political economy

“. And the question I keep circling is whether this movement is best understood as a crisis

for

 Kenyan Christianity or as, in some sense, an event

within

 it – i.e. not an attack from outside the tradition but an argument the tradition is having, urgently and in public, with itself.


This educated, digitally connected youth demographic had identified religious institutions as central pillars sustaining the oppressive political order. Youth activists asserted that

church leaders had become complicit in state oppression

 by accepting money from corrupt politicians, surrendering sacred altars to political actors, and maintaining silence in a time of severe economic distress. 


The political economy of extractive ministry and elite patronage


Religious authority in Kenya, and across much of the continent, has for decades functioned less as a moral counterweight to power than as its most reliable subcontractor. The alliance is old and almost structurally inevitable – a state that cannot always be trusted to deliver services will always find it convenient to borrow legitimacy from an institution that promises something even the state cannot: salvation, certainty, a story of individual transformation that, however politically convenient for elites, is also, for the person living it, a genuine and often quite beautiful thing. Pentecostal and Charismatic movements provide essential social networks, existential security, and personal empowerment in urban environments plagued by severe inequality and state neglect. Through

emphasis on personal transformation, moral discipline, and individual efficacy,

 churches equip believers with practical survival strategies to navigate economic precarity. 


However, most of these movements operate under a “

Prosperity Gospel

” theology, a framework that interprets material wealth and physical well-being as direct indicators of divine favour unlocked through financial contributions. Originating from international Pentecostal currents and adapting to indigenous spiritual frameworks,

prosperity theology centres on seed-sowing economics

. In this transactional framework, congregants are urged to yield financial offerings to church proprietors to activate supernatural returns.

Where institutional financial records remain opaque and unregulated, extractive ministry thrives

. Capital generated from millions of socio-economically marginalized adherents is accumulated tax-free by religious elites who showcase luxury assets and extravagant personal lifestyles. This accumulation model operates through a psychological apparatus that spiritualizes structural poverty, framing systemic economic failures as personal spiritual deficits resulting from insufficient faith or inadequate financial giving.


The financial imperatives of extractive religious institutions create a structural convergence with the political class. Political figures have

routinely leveraged the pulpit

 to secure political legitimacy, purchase moral sanitization, and gain access to voting blocs. In exchange for substantial cash donations to church building funds and public fundraisers, politicians are granted access to church platforms during weekend services. From these sacred altars, political elites advance electoral agendas, defend unpopular policies, and evade accountability for corruption and governance failures.


This dynamic was

prominently demonstrated

 in Kenya during the consolidation of President William Ruto’s administration. Tracing his political trajectory from youth evangelism in the North Rift Evangelistic Team to his presidential campaigns, Ruto deployed Pentecostal language and networks to build a powerful political coalition. Framed as a spiritual battle of the poor “hustlers” against elite dynasties, his political strategy relied heavily on church prayer rallies, frequent endorsements by evangelical prelates, and public declarations that his electoral triumph was a divine mandate. Following his election, this

Pentecostalization of statecraft

 was institutionalized through regular interdenominational prayer services inside the State House, diplomatic prayer …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Zakariae Azennoud
title: Hijra: Movement, Migration, and Islamic Thought
content:
The question of why 70,000 Moroccans migrated to the Spanish-governed territories of Ceuta and Melilla within hours on 30 July – ‘Throne Day’, which is one of the most respectable celebrations of the Morocco Kingdom – still lingers in international media and haunts inquisitive minds. Commentators have talked extensively about the socio-economic and geopolitical incentives, but the underreported in coverage seems to lie within the subjective semantics of

hijra

itself, the Arabic word for

migration

, its connotation in the Arabo-Islamic context, and therefore in the collective perception of the Arabs and/or Muslims, including Moroccans.


The word

hijra

 occurs twenty-four times in the Qur’an, the holy scripture of Muslims. All cases manifest in a positive, favourable context. Speaking about verbs in particular, the verb

hājara

(to migrate) occurs sixteen times, around fourteen of which denote a voluntary and lovable act. The Qur’an reads: “And whoever migrates for the cause of Allah will find on the earth many [alternative] locations and abundance” (4:100). The Qur’an is the primary representative of the standard Arabic language, so meanings of cognate words like

hijra

, vernacular usage included, are derived from it.


Ceuta is a Spanish exclave adjoining Moroccan territory.


Muslim countries follow the

Hijri

 calendar for religious observance even though it is decreasingly used in everyday professional life. The calendar’s first date, approximately 16 July 622 AD, marks the Prophet Muhammad’s migration from Mecca, where he spent thirteen years spreading the faith of Islam, to Medina, where the Islamic civil society was instituted.

al-muhājirūn

, Mecca migrants (versus

al-’ansār

, the Helpers, or native Medinese, who had been themselves migrants from South Arabia), are identified as the companions of the Prophet who stood by him in the previous mission. In the early years of Islam, by the approval of the Prophet, two migrations took place from Mecca to Abyssinia, modern-day northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, and had impactful result on the spreading of Islam at the time. The Prophet Muhammad approved these movements due to the continuous persecution of his followers by his tribe the Quraysh in Mecca and his hope to find a just land that would consider his prophethood. The migrants in Abyssinia practiced and preached their religion freely; some of them were extremely impressed by the justice and freedom provided by the leader, even one of the migrants converted to Christianity and stayed there for the rest of his life.


Many years after the inception of the

Hijri

 calendar,

muhājirūn

 found new home and lived in Medina forever. One great success attributed to the Prophet by his biographers is the preeminent ability to tie a brothering bond between

al-muhājirūn

 and

al-’ansār

 – and a little while before, between

al-’ansār

 tribal groups such as the Arab

’aws

 and

khazraj

– and thereby a foundation of an emerging powerful state was enabled. “The Hijra demolishes what preceded it”, said the Prophet Muhammad to a companion called Amr ibn al-As, which possibly means that a migrant has to promote a new living experience (seeking heaven) and cut ties with a previous (heathen) one if it proves to be deficient.


The overwhelming majority of Moroccans, about 98% of the population, are Muslims and Islam is the religion of the nation by constitution. The learnings they accumulate through schooling and self-navigation of knowledge combined render

hijra

 a culturally-loaded act infused with positive signification. Numerous present-day aspirant migrants may not conjure up, in clear reminiscence, all these cultural thoughts, but such implications as highlighted earlier are rooted in the collective memory of Moroccans.


The number of Moroccan diaspora in Spain increased recently to a million. There is also currently another million in Italy, half a million in France, a million in Belgium and the Netherlands, even as far as the Middle East, there are about a million Moroccan-origin Israelis. By this measure, international Moroccan demographics help naturalise

hijra

 by accentuating previous successes. From a chronological standpoint, the Moroccan identity is said to have been formed at the intersection of historic civilizations: Berber, Sahrawi, and Andalusian; with regard to the latter, Morocco was the nearest place in which the Arabs, Muslims, and Jews displaced from Andalusia found refuge. History …

author: Thaer Abu Aoun, Mahmoud Bashir
title: Israeli military abducts Gaza City Interior Ministry official in raid
content:
The Israeli military abducted an internal security apparatus officer, Muain al-Arabid, during a raid on Gaza City, the Palestinian Interior Ministry

announced

 Tuesday.

 


Arabid was carrying out his regular duties when the Israeli special forces unit infiltrated the Katiba area, west of Gaza City, according to the statement, which said he was injured during a clash with the unit.


The attack killed Arabid’s wife and injured several of his children, with Palestinian newspaper Al-Ayyam

reporting

 Wednesday that the clash killed four people in total, including two children.


While Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli military claimed that Arabid is a “senior Hamas figure” who had been pushing to restore Hamas’ control over northern Gaza, Hamas official Mohamed Madhoun denied the allegations, saying that Arabid worked within Gaza’s governmental security apparatus. 


The abduction is another instance of Israel’s continued targeting of police and other service institutions in Gaza, said Madhoun. 


An eyewitness in the Katiba area at the time of Tuesday’s attack recounted to Mada Masr that a closed white truck arrived at the scene before several armed individuals disembarked from the vehicle to storm a house, barricading themselves inside before opening heavy fire on people outside. 


Israeli aircraft simultaneously carried out approximately ten strikes in under five minutes, the witness added.


Another eyewitness described the infiltrating force withdrawing in a jeep amid the bombardment shortly before an airstrike targeted the white truck the force had used to reach the area.


The Interior Ministry also said the Israeli unit entered the area in civilian vehicles before exploiting a heavy airstrike campaign to escape. 


A Gaza-based outlet affiliated with Hamas’ security, Al-Hares,

quoted

 an unnamed security source

saying

 that the “resistance thwarted an offensive that targeted a key leadership figure while the Occupation succeeded in kidnapping a security official who was present at the scene of the operation.”

 


The same source said that “resistance forces detected the Israeli unit, inflicted casualties and seized some of its weapons and equipment,” adding that it had also apprehended and arrested three people who were providing the Israeli force assistance with intelligence gathering. 


The director of Gaza’s Government Media Office also

said

 that several members of the Israeli special forces were killed after their presence was discovered, prompting the deployment of more than 10 aircraft to carry out the series of heavy strikes.


The Israeli military, however,

denied

 that any of the special forces personnel had been wounded.


Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile,

said

 the operation had resulted in the capture of Hamas’ internal security service head near his home in central Gaza City, alleging that Arabid had been involved in concealing and transferring Israeli hostages and in efforts to restore Hamas’ capabilities.


The Occupation military also

claimed

 Arabid had recently been working to promote attacks against Israeli troops operating near the Yellow Line.


Hamas official Mohamed al-Madhoun told Mada Masr that Arabid had no role in transferring Israeli prisoners and that he is part of the government security apparatus and does not work in Hamas’s military wing


Arabid’s duties included protecting the population in Gaza and maintaining internal security against thieves, criminal gangs and agents, said Madhoun.


The ministry said in its statement that Arabid had been “undertaking his normal responsibilities, part of doing his duty in the service of our people and preserving the civil peace in the Gaza Strip,” linking the operation to what it described as the occupation’s objective of “shattering and dismantling the security apparatus and spreading chaos” — a goal it stated has persisted since the aggression began over three years ago and has intensified since the ceasefire

agreement

 reached in October of last year.


According to earlier

data

 from the ministry, Israel has killed 61 police officers since the ceasefire. The most recent casualties included eight Palestinian police officers — among them the governorate’s police chief, Brigadier General Ayman Jandiya — killed in the middle of last month during a strike on the municipal police headquarters in the Gaza Governorate. Jandiya had assumed his post only two weeks prior …

author: ROAPE
title: The murder of Professor Jason Arday
content:
On Sunday 16 August I joined the vigil for Professor Arday in London’s Trafalgar Square in the summer’s heat, packed tight with thousands of protestors marking their respect, holding bunches of flowers aloft, and placards reading, ‘Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday.’ Heads bowed, hundreds around me in tears – the words of his students unbearable, our anger craving a response. 


Professor Arday is dead. Murdered. Yet again another Black person has been killed – pilloried in a public execution orchestrated by a profoundly racist press, and organised fascists.


The vigil spoke to the structural racism that shaped Professor Arday’s life and death. I was struck by British MP Diane Abbott’s comments on the Black experience in the UK and the racism encountered daily. This daily experience is engrained in British institutions, the press and political life.


His family commented about the outpouring of grief and fury, describing their emotions: ‘The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.’


Bittersweet indeed – the kindness, support and grief were essential but too late. 


Professor Jason Arday – the Black professor of sociology at Cambridge University – was hounded to his death by a racist campaign to unseat him from his position. In the 22 days leading to his suicide, there were 249 articles in major newspapers in the UK, continual coverage on TV, radio and blogs. This had followed a repeated effort to undermine Arday since he became a professor at the university in 2023.


The noise from this pogrom – accusing him of plagiarism, lies, bombast, academic fakery – was overwhelming. Many people who should have known better joined the chorus. The UK’s mainstream liberal paper, 

The Guardian,

 

launched an investigation into Arday’s scholarship

. I encountered family members who joined in the chorus – denouncing Arday, ridiculing his claims, and his work.


On 5 August, Arday resigned from his post; the following week, on 14 August, he committed suicide. A man described by his students as ‘gentle’, ‘caring’, ‘compassionate’ and ‘inspiring’ was systematically broken – destroyed in a campaign which led directly to his suicide. 


Arday was murdered. 


This was the objective – Arday’s suicide was the logical outcome. Leading the recent crusade was the racist scholar, Nathan Cofnas, who published on his Substack the blog, ‘

DEI Fraud and Cover-Up at Cambridge

’, on 21 July 2026.  A vile man who targeted and conducted his own investigation into Arday’s work  – charging him with plagiarism, which confirmed Cofnas’ thesis that Black people are inferior, unworthy of senior academic positions. 


Cofnas is a symptom of our times. A marginal, bigoted voice that once would have remained largely undetected in the swamp is now amplified by a mainstream, racist agenda. In the global North, these voices have reached fever pitch – finding traction in a political climate that has seen right-wing governments elected, and racist policies normalised in daily political speech. 


To say these developments are worrying is a grotesque understatement – these are clarion signs of our current and deepening crisis, and the irredeemable racism of our political and economic system. This cannot be absorbed and understood simply as a British thing. We see the same tightening of the screw in the personal attacks on International Criminal Court judges and the normalisation of genocide.


There are three observations that I want to make in this piece. Firstly, I want to look at two political parallels –  one that prompted the global mass movement, Black Lives Matter, a few years ago, and the second when antisemitism was denounced by the French author Émile Zola at the end of the 19

th

 century. Finally, I want to say a few things about plagiarism and academia. 


On 25 May 2020 in Minneapolis, George Floyd was stopped by the police, then wrestled to the ground by police officer Derek Chauvin – clips of his slow death over nine minutes were beamed across the planet. Chauvin was later convicted of murder. George Floyd was choked to death by Chauvin, who pinned Floyd to the ground, as he died – filmed by the incredibly brave 17-year-old Darnella Frazie – he was heard saying,‘Mama, mama, mama’, ‘Momma, I love you,’ and ‘Momma! I’m through.’

author: Nyambura Mundia
title: Faith and Fury: How Moral Populism Became Kenya’s Political Currency
content:
Religion has never been peripheral to Kenyan politics. Churches have provided welfare, organized communities and challenged governments; they have also offered political leaders networks of influence and a language of moral legitimacy. The relationship has never been straightforward. Religious authority has, at different moments, been used to reinforce political power and to confront it.


What deserves attention now is not the presence of faith in politics, but the changing relationship between religious authority and political legitimacy.


William Ruto did not introduce Christianity into Kenya’s political life. Nor did he invent the longstanding practice of politicians cultivating religious constituencies. What is distinctive about his presidency is the prominence of his own born-again identity within the exercise and symbolism of political office. His political biography is repeatedly narrated through faith, providence and renewal; his presidency has cultivated visible relationships with Christian leaders and institutions, particularly within evangelical and Pentecostal circles; and religious symbolism has increasingly accompanied the performance of presidential authority.


The question is not whether religion belongs in Kenyan public life. It plainly does. Nor is it whether Christians should bring their convictions into politics. They should. The harder question is what happens when religious authority moves beyond participation in political contestation and begins to furnish political power with an additional claim to legitimacy.


In Kenya, that question has acquired concrete form. Prayer has become part of the symbolism surrounding the presidency. Religious leaders have maintained close access to political power. Financial relationships between politicians and churches have raised questions about influence and patronage. And proposals to establish religious institutions within state spaces have raised a more fundamental question about the boundary between the faith of an officeholder and the institutional character of the state.


None of this makes Kenya a theocracy. Nor does it make Christian institutions a single political bloc. The church has never spoken with one voice, and religious actors have continued to challenge as well as support political authority.


But it does expose a tension at the heart of democratic politics: how can deeply held religious convictions shape public life without allowing any particular interpretation of those convictions to become the measure of political legitimacy?


That is the question this essay explores. Because moral populism does not require faith to enter politics. It requires moral authority to become political currency.


The sacramental logic of power


Political authority has rarely been purely secular. Rulers have long sought legitimacy not only through law, institutions and force, but also through claims about morality, tradition and the sacred. Christianity became embedded in the institutions and social structures through which colonial rule was organized, while postcolonial states across Africa have continued to negotiate the relationship between constitutional authority, religious institutions and public morality.


Kenya’s political history reflects this complexity. Churches have not simply been instruments of political power. They have been schools, welfare providers, mediators, and important sites of civic organization. They have also moved between proximity to political authority and resistance to it. During the authoritarian years, sections of the church worked alongside the state on questions of welfare and national cohesion, while others became increasingly critical of one-party rule. By the late 1980s and 1990s, clergy such as Anglican bishops David Gitari and Henry Okullu, Presbyterian minister Timothy Njoya and Catholic bishop Ndingi Mwana-a Nzeki were among the religious leaders using sermons, church networks, and public advocacy to challenge political repression and press for democratic reform. The National Council of Churches of Kenya also became an important institutional voice in the struggle for political and constitutional change.


That history matters because it complicates any simple account of religion and power. The church has not occupied a fixed political position in Kenya. Religious authority has at different moments been used to reinforce political order and to challenge it. The same pulpit that can lend moral weight to political …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies: A Community of Practice to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence
content:
Over the past year, Liberation Alliance Africa has sustained the

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Indigenous Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

. This Community of Practice is a collective of African feminist scholars, practitioners, organisers, artists, and movement builders committed to the dreaming and making of a world free from sexual violence through knowledge bridges.


Sexual violence continues to impact communities across the African continent, and class, ethnicity and religion play a critical role in making civilians in conflict-affected countries particularly more vulnerable. It disproportionately affects women and girls, and ethnic, gender and racialized minorities. Sexual violence is compounded by conflict, displacement, poverty, and gender inequality. It remains significantly under-reported due to stigma and under-prosecuted? Due to weak and corrupt justice systems. Sexual violence includes rape and sexual assault, sexual coercion and exploitation, including trafficking for sexual exploitation and conflict-related sexual violence such as using rape as a weapon of war. It affects people of any gender and age. 


Our starting premise is simple: sexual violence on the continent cannot be understood, let alone addressed, through frameworks that treat colonialism as history rather than a structural force that continues to shape theory, practice, and response to sexual violence. 


Coloniality was

coined

by Peruvian philosopher and sociologist Aníbal Quijano, and it describes the long-lasting pattern of power produced by colonial rule and shape

s

 how we approach epistemological frameworks through which violence is understood.

Epistemology deals with questions concerning the nature, scope, and sources of knowledge.

 A meaningful analysis of sexual violence must begin by seeking to decolonise knowledge and epistemic structures. This analysis requires us to interrogate the assumptions that underpin dominant theories, question whose expertise is legitimised, and create space for African feminist epistemologies to shape how violence is understood, prevented, and responded to. 


We felt an urgent need to organise as scholars and practitioners to generate new frameworks grounded in our histories, political realities, and lived experiences. Our analyses are rooted in our confrontation of the neo-colonial state, the global imperialist, extractive and patriarchal systems that shape our everyday existence. We arrive as feminists in service of a liberatory project, convinced that knowledge-making is itself a site of feminist struggle. 


As the CoP came together through both intentional convening and organic growth, we began organising our work around three enquiries that we believe are critical to envisioning a decolonial feminist approach to preventing and responding to sexual violence in Africa. 


The first enquiry,

Whose Knowledge? An Audit of the Current Knowledge Systems within Sexual Violence Prevention and Response in Africa

 examines the dominant literature, asks whose voices have shaped the field, whose knowledge has been marginalised, and what becomes possible when African feminist scholarship is placed at the centre of analysis. 


The second enquiry,

 The Coloniality of Sexual Violence: Gender, Power, Sovereignty, and the Neo-Colonial State,

 advances interventions on sexual violence that explicitly interrogate the role and impact of hetero-patriarchal colonial racial-capitalism, alongside the complicity of neo-colonial states, in producing and sustaining conditions of gendered violence. 


The third enquiry,

Truth-telling and Epistemic Sovereignty in the Prevention and Response Continuum

, centres on indigenous and endogenous knowledge systems as essential practice-based frameworks for reimagining prevention, response, healing, accountability, and collective safety.


The Imperative of Recentering African Epistemologies


At Liberation Alliance Africa, we believe African women and gender-expansive people’s knowledge-making and world-building are crucial to de-westernising normative assumptions and dominant approaches. African women and gender-expansive scholars must nurture new ways of knowing and being- knowledge that doesn’t just challenge dominant views, but creates a rich foundation for how we understand reality and tackle life’s critical questions.


For a long time, African women and gender minorities were treated as …

author: WoMin
title: On Language and the Pedagogy of Liberation
content:
Across Africa, colonialism was not only a project of economic exploitation and political domination; it was also a project of language and cultural control. Colonial rule sought to determine not only who governed and who had access to resources but also elevated European languages as symbols of intelligence and authority, while African languages were systematically marginalised. 


African literature captured this contradiction. In

So Long a Letter

, Mariama Bâ writes from within the tensions of expressing African women’s realities through a language inherited from colonial rule. Ama Ata Aidoo’s novel

Our Sister Killjoy

, similarly, exposes the uneasy relationship between English as a language of literary expression and also as a reminder of cultural displacement. These reflections continue to resonate with present-day realities across the continent, where language remains deeply entangled with questions of power, culture, identity, class, gender, and belonging.  


Today, access to education, legal systems, government services, and political participation in many African countries still depends heavily on competence in colonial languages such as English, French, or Portuguese.  


In Nigeria, for example, although more than 250 languages are spoken across the country, English remains the dominant language of governance, education or even policy discourse. Similar dynamics persist elsewhere on the continent. In Tanzania, although Kiswahili is the national language, many court judgments continue to be delivered in English. Citizens who do not understand English must depend on interpreters to comprehend legal decisions affecting their lives. 


For peasant and working-class women confronting mining, oil extraction, logging, large-scale agricultural investments, and other extractive projects, language exclusions carry profound consequences especially for rural women whose language is deeply tied to their relationship to land, water, forests, food systems, ancestry, and survival.  


Where information about government-proposed projects is often delivered in foreign languages without clarifying their implications including the terms of the proposed project, the risks it poses, the compensation being offered, or the legal mechanisms available to challenge it, their ability to give meaningful consent or organise resistance against it, then language becomes a question of power. 


Language in Women Learning Liberation and Translation as a Tool of Resistance

 


Language was central to the development of

Women Learning Liberation

  (WLL), WoMin’s 18-month political education course for frontline women activists. The first WLL cohort began in July 2024, bringing together 60 women from Cameroon, Guinea Conakry, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, South Africa, and Uganda. From the beginning, WLL understood political education not as the transfer of knowledge from experts to communities, but as a process of collective learning rooted in women’s own experiences and struggles. 


The Ugandan WLL cohort spoke eight languages and represented five different community struggles. English could provide a common language for some discussions, but relying exclusively on it would have risked excluding women from fully expressing their experiences, questions, analysis, and political imagination. WLL therefore deliberately incorporated interpretation into the political education process. Facilitation moved between English, Luganda, Runyoro, and Kinyarwanda, while participants themselves became active in ensuring that interpretation was taking place. 


As

Ugandan facilitator Sostine Namanya

 explained: “Language can work, but language needs to be budgeted for, language needs to be prepped for.” 


In many African contexts, people come from diverse language backgrounds and often speak multiple languages. While English or French may serve as common languages, reliance on colonial languages can reproduce unequal power relations and weaken movements. Interpretation and translation therefore become powerful tools for building multilingual and robust movements capable of deepening collective participation.  


In 2024, WoMin launched materials supporting the

Right To Say NO  campaign in East Africa

 in five languages, which join a plethora of knowledge materials and resources such as its award-winning film,

Women Hold up the Sky

 (2021) and a comic book,

Voices against Extractivism: Sheroes for Change

. The act of interpretation and …

author: Gary Chartier
title: Pro-Pasar, Anti-“Kapitalisme”
content:
Gary Chartier

. Teks aslinya berjudul ‘

Embracing Markets, Opposing “Capitalism

”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa


Menjadi seorang libertarian berarti menolak penggunaan kekerasan untuk membatasi pertukaran yang berlangsung secara damai dan sukarela. Namun, hal itu tidak berarti bahwa libertarianisme harus dipahami sebagai dukungan terhadap kapitalisme.


Apakah klaim ini masuk akal atau tidak, tentu bergantung pada apa yang Anda maksud dengan “kapitalisme”. Bagi sebagian orang, mungkin istilah tersebut sekadar merujuk pada pertukaran bebas. Jika memang itu yang Anda maksud ketika berbicara tentang “kapitalisme”, Anda benar bahwa tidak ada pertentangan nyata antara apa yang Anda maksud dan libertarianisme yang masuk akal.


Namun, ketika menggunakan istilah tersebut, orang sering kali memiliki pengertian lain dalam pikirannya. Misalnya, media cetak dan elektronik arus utama secara rutin menggunakan “kapitalisme” untuk merujuk pada “sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini”. Cukup umum pula mendengar “kapitalisme” digunakan sebagai sinonim dari “dominasi kapitalis atas tempat kerja dan masyarakat – yakni dominasi oleh para pemilik aset modal dalam jumlah besar”. Prinsip-prinsip libertarian, sebagaimana saya memahaminya, tidak mengharuskan dukungan terhadap kapitalisme dalam kedua pengertian tersebut.


Dalam tingkat yang sangat signifikan

, sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini justru merupakan sistem yang di dalamnya pertukaran damai dan sukarela tidak sepenuhnya hadir. Jaringan hak istimewa yang dibentuk oleh hukum dan regulasi saling terkait memberikan keuntungan kepada orang-orang kaya dan mereka yang memiliki koneksi politik, dengan mengorbankan orang lain (misalnya paten dan hak cipta, tarif, pembatasan perbankan, aturan perizinan profesi, pembatasan penggunaan lahan, dan sebagainya). Kompleks industri-militer mengalirkan uang dalam jumlah yang sulit dipercaya – dengan todongan senjata – dari kantong masyarakat biasa ke rekening para kontraktor pemerintah dan kroni-kroninya. Berbagai bentuk subsidi memberi makan jaringan hak istimewa bagi perusahaan maupun organisasi nirlaba. Negara juga melindungi kepemilikan atas tanah yang diperoleh dengan todongan senjata atau dikuasai melalui keputusan sepihak sebelum kemudian dibagikan kepada individu dan kelompok yang disukai. Memang, setidaknya perekonomian Amerika Serikat, Kanada, Eropa Barat, Jepang, dan Australia bukanlah perekonomian yang direncanakan secara terpusat. Negara juga tidak secara formal mengklaim kepemilikan atas (sebagian besar) alat-alat produksi. Namun, keterlibatan negara di berbagai tingkat dalam menjamin dan memperkuat hak-hak istimewa ekonomi membuat sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini sulit disebut sebagai sistem yang bebas. Jadi, jika “kapitalisme” digunakan untuk menyebut sistem yang kita miliki sekarang, siapa pun yang mendukung kebebasan memiliki alasan kuat untuk bersikap skeptis terhadap kapitalisme.


Hak-hak istimewa yang menjadi ciri tatanan ekonomi yang ada saat ini, apa pun nama yang kita gunakan untuk menyebutnya, secara tidak proporsional menguntungkan mereka yang memiliki pengaruh politik paling besar dan kekayaan paling besar. Jaringan hak istimewa yang dipertahankan oleh negara juga, dalam berbagai cara, cenderung memperkuat posisi istimewa para kapitalis di tempat kerja. Dalam konteks tempat kerja, hak istimewa yang dijamin negara mengurangi kemungkinan orang untuk bekerja secara mandiri (dengan meningkatkan kebutuhan modal dan berbagai biaya masuk lainnya, sekaligus mengurangi sumber daya yang mungkin dapat digunakan seseorang untuk memulai dan mempertahankan usahanya sendiri). Negara juga memberlakukan pembatasan terhadap aktivitas serikat pekerja yang mengurangi kemampuan pekerja untuk melakukan tawar-menawar secara efektif dengan pemberi kerja. Dengan mengurangi alternatif selain pekerjaan berupah dan mempersempit peluang pekerja untuk melakukan perundingan kolektif, negara secara substansial meningkatkan daya tawar pemberi kerja. Singkatnya, dominasi “kapitalis” atas tempat kerja dan masyarakat tidak dapat dipahami dalam bentuknya yang sekarang tanpa memperhatikan campur tangan dan penyimpangan yang dilakukan negara. Sekali lagi, jika inilah yang disebut “kapitalisme”, para pendukung kebebasan tidak memiliki alasan untuk menerimanya.


Tentu saja, masuk akal jika seseorang berpendapat bahwa meskipun “kapitalisme” sering digunakan untuk merujuk pada fenomena sosial yang patut dipersoalkan …

author: Sav Jonsa
title: Manitoba officers charged in just 2% of all police-involved deaths since 2015
content:
This is the first part in a series focused on the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba. Stay tuned for part two.


The police watchdog responsible for investigating all officer-involved deaths in Manitoba has never met its mandate of accountability, transparency and independence, says a man who helped establish it more than a decade ago.


A months-long IJF [Investigative Journalism Foundation] probe into its history found the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba, or IIU, has charged Manitoba police officers in only two per cent of all police-involved deaths since becoming active in 2015. As well, the IIU hasn’t publicly released annual reports for the last three fiscal years, its website is often inaccessible to the public and the IIU has been operating without a permanent civilian director since late 2024.


The information is frustrating for Robert Taman, who believed police accountability was headed in the “right direction” when he first helped establish the IIU in the early 2010s. It was created by the province after

police botched the 2005 investigation into his wife Crystal’s death

 in a crash with an off-duty officer.


Crystal Taman, a 40-year-old Métis woman and mother of three children, was known as the ‘heart of the family.’ Photo: Taman Inquiry.


Now 11 years since its launch, Taman saidys he sees a lack of transparency and independence at the IIU, which is “completely against what it was meant to be.”


“I don’t think they’ve ever met their mandate,” said Taman. “I believe that everybody’s intentions are correct and they’re all trying to do the right thing, but in the end it’s like they get to a certain point and they can’t go any further.”


Taman’s skepticism of the IIU has also been shared by many

Indigenous community members and advocacy organizations

 in Manitoba after the IIU declined charging officers in several death investigations of First Nations people, notably in the cases of

Eishia Hudson

, 16,

Janine Walker

, 23,

James Wood

, 35,

John Ettawakapow

, 54,

Tammy Bateman

, 39, and

Elias Whitehead

, 37, to name just a few.


Whitehead died after his arrest in 2023 by the Winnipeg Police Service, who were responding to a call about a man “acting erratically in traffic” near the city’s downtown.


Whitehead was unarmed.


The

IIU’s final report for his death investigation

 states that during his arrest, officers punched Whitehead approximately 23 times in the head and body and delivered three knee strikes to his body. The autopsy found his cause of death to be “subdual and prone restraint (by police officers) complicating cocaine intoxication and cardiomegaly (enlarged heart).”


His common-law wife, Jody Beardy, told the IJF that officers not being charged in his death “didn’t make sense.”


“The IIU … I don’t know what their point is when they do not hold [police] responsible for what they did, what they do,” said Beardy, who had to wait more than two years after Whitehead’s death to learn no charges would be laid through the investigation.


Elias Whitehead is pictured here with his common-law wife, Jody Beardy. She posted several photos of Whitehead soon after he died in police-custody, saying that her ‘heart is completely broken’ and that she now has to ‘live in this world alone without the love of my life!’ Photo courtesy Jody Beardy.


According to its website, the IIU’s mandate ensures accountability, independence, objectivity, high investigative standards, timeliness, thoroughness and transparency in its investigations. Police must notify the IIU whenever there is an incident it may need to investigate. They do not take public complaints.


The IJF examined about 1,000 publicly available IIU documents, including news releases, annual reports and final reports, to find trends in their investigations, which include all death, serious injury and criminal allegations against officers for every police service in Manitoba including the RCMP, municipal police and First Nations police forces.


Since annual reports summarizing IIU investigations were not available for the last three years, the IJF had to pull data from close to 350 individual news releases from April 2023 onward.


There may be information not shared publicly by the IIU that the IJF was unable to record.


The IJF’s research found police officers have been charged in only two out of roughly 100 concluded death investigations since the IIU’s inception, according to published annual reports and news …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: 33 Democrats Vote to Withhold Funding From Universities That Boycott Israel
content:
The bill would not even allow institutions to take actions to limit commercial deals with Israel.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The House voted on Thursday to pass a bipartisan bill that would cut off federal funding for universities that participate in a boycott of Israel, with dozens of Democrats in favor.

The bill passed 237 to 169, with almost all Republicans and 33 Democrats voting in favor. Democrats who voted “yes” included some of the most vocally pro-Israel and conservative lawmakers in the caucus. It now goes to the Senate for consideration.

Further, Democrats were complicit in allowing the vote to go forth to begin with. On Tuesday, Representatives Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Washington), both Democrats, surprised caucus leaders when they voted for the GOP’s rule to allow the consideration of several pieces of legislation to go forth — a highly unusual move that delivered House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) the votes he needed to advance the rule.

This included votes on the anti-boycott bill as well as a resolution calling for the passage of Republicans’ voter suppression legislation and condemning the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and socialism “in all its forms.” That resolution passed with 8 Democrats in favor. Golden and Perez voted for both.

The anti-boycott legislation, called the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act, would amend the Higher Education Act of 1965 to prohibit institutions of higher education from ending or even taking steps to limit commercial relations with Israel that aren’t “based on a valid business reason.” Institutions wouldn’t even be able to boycott entities like illegal Israeli settlements under the legislation.

It also requires schools to prove that students and faculty are not “reasonably obstructed” from participating in academic exchange programs with Israel. If an institution fails either of those checks, it would lose federal funding under the bill.

Many universities are deeply intertwined with Israel; recent reports found, for instance, that the Israeli military is funding and collaborating on at least 70 research projects across U.S. universities. Colleges and universities maintain exchange programs, conduct academic research collaborations, and are even financially intertwined with Israel. The Palestine solidarity movement, by contrast, calls for universities to cut off Israel and participate in an academic boycott similar to the academic boycott of apartheid South Africa.

The measure was introduced by Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx (North Carolina) as well as conservative Democrat Rep. Josh Gottheimer (New Jersey), who said that the bill is necessary to combat the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement on campuses.

Gottheimer claimed that the bill “doesn’t touch anyone’s speech, protest, or academic debate,” even though a crucial goal of many left-wing and pro-Palestine student groups, especially amid the genocide in Gaza, has been to urge their universities to boycott Israel.

Critics have said that the bill is aimed at suppressing speech critical of Israel.

The Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act “is designed to repress free speech and compromise institutional independence and academic freedom by applying political pressure on universities to prevent any consideration of any potential boycotts of the state of Israel,” said lobbying group A New Policy in a statement last year, when the bill was first introduced.

Notably, Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott (Virginia) observed during committee markup of the bill that “there has not been a single case of an American college or university administration adopting the BDS movement policies that are described in the bill.”

Indeed, many prominent colleges and universities have instead harshly punished students who participated in protests against the U.S.’s complicity with Israel’s genocide in Gaza; some of them even deepened their relationships with Israel after the protests.

The legislation, if passed, would represent an expansion of laws aimed at suppressing pro-Palestine speech. At least 38 states have some form of legislation combatting individuals’ or businesses’ ability to participate in boycotts of Israel.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: FMF Staff
title: Statement of the Feminist Majority Foundation on the Death of Gloria Steinem
content:
Gloria Steinem, a lifelong champion of women’s equality and co-founder of Ms. magazine, died Sept. 2, 2026, at age 92. For more than half a century, Steinem helped bring feminist ideas, voices and movements into the mainstream through journalism, organizing and activism—and helped build Ms. into what it remains today: not simply a magazine, but a movement.

“When Steinem and the other owners of Ms. entrusted the magazine to the Feminist Majority Foundation, we understood that we were being entrusted with far more than a publication,” said Katherine Spillar, executive director of Feminist Majority Foundation and executive editor of Ms. “We were being asked to preserve an independent feminist institution, and to keep it alive, questioning and relevant for generations that would face battles we could not yet foresee. That responsibility is more urgent today than at any time in recent memory.”

Today, Ms. magazine is thriving. In print and online it reaches tens of thousands of readers every day and over 4.5 million readers a year. It has not only maintained consistent print circulation throughout the pandemic and the overall decline of print media, but has also seen its web presence skyrocket through its website, social media, and the podcasts it publishes through Ms. Studio. Ms. can also be found in thousands of libraries and classrooms, where new generations encounter feminist journalism, history and ideas that might otherwise never reach them.

“Gloria understood the importance of independent feminist media from the beginning,” said Eleanor Smeal, publisher of Ms. and president of the Feminist Majority Foundation. “Ms. remains an independent, nonprofit, feminist newsroom that is not beholden to commercial advertisers. That independence allows Ms. to keep breaking new ground, just as Gloria intended. From reproductive freedom and violence against women to pay equity, political representation and the global struggle for human rights, Ms. continues to cover the issues affecting women long before much of the mainstream media recognizes their importance.”

Ms. Magazine was co-founded in 1972 by Gloria Steinem. Gloria asked the Feminist Majority Foundation to take over Ms. magazine, and the Feminist Majority Foundation has been the publisher of Ms. magazine since 2001.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Lori Idlout regrets expenses made while she was NDP MP
content:
Nunavut MP Lori Idlout agreed she made an error in judgement after a report released Wednesday concluded that expenses she claimed in 2024 and 2025 constituted a conflict of interest.


The purchases made by her member’s office constituted an error in judgement, Canada’s Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein found after his investigation into the incident, but he didn’t impose any sanctions against her, noting her errors were made in “good faith.”


The expenses included

four

 occasions when her staff bought gifts from Carvings Nunavut, a retail art gallery where she is the sole shareholder and director. 


As well, the report looks into accommodations the MP booked at a bed and breakfast in Igloolik owned by her spouse Allan Mullin. 


“As soon as these were brought to my attention, I immediately reimbursed all these claimed expenses, demonstrating a true desire to fully rectify these errors,” the MP said in a public statement following the report’s publication. 


“I did not consider that these purchases made for legitimate parliamentary purposes would further private interests, as I receive no income from the businesses in question,” she added. “I have since learned from this experience.”


The purchases were all made prior to her

crossing the floor

 to join the Liberals, when she was an NDP MP.


“Idlout reimbursed all of the claimed expenses immediately after the concerns were brought to her attention,” the commissioner wrote in his report. “In my view, this demonstrated a true desire on Ms. Idlout’s part to fully rectify each of her past non-compliances.”


Finckenstein came to that conclusion after Idlout testified that, though she owns Carvings Nunavut, she does not financially benefit from its operations, nor does she take part in its day to day operations.


Idlout has not received any income from the business, which buys and sells Inuit art such as carvings and prints, since before she was elected, according to the commissioner.


She testified that any surplus generated from the sale of art after staff salaries, rent, bills and other operation costs goes toward purchasing more art. 


The largest expenditure from Carvings Nunavut involved $1,380 in sculptures, cards, tote bags, hand-crafted keychains and zipper pulls, gifted to First Nations leaders, elders and other speakers at the NDP’s national caucus meeting in British Columbia, in September 2025.


The three other gifts were all under $200. They were given to

Rebecca Chartrand, minister of northern and Arctic affairs; Greg Fergus, former speaker of the House of Commons, during visits to Iqaluit; and to staff at the Kivalliq Long-Term Care Elders Centre, to celebrate the

completion

 of the project in Rankin Inlet.  


As for the travel expenses involving her spouse’s business, Al’s B&B in Igloolik, Finckenstein noted the stay was disclosed

 right after a trip in March 2025, and the MP’s choice resulted from a lack of other available accommodations. 


Idlout and two staffers had initially hoped to book rooms at a

hotel in Sanirajak, a small community about 70 kilometres from Igloolik where Idlout was hosting an event, but the hotel was fully booked. With the hotel in Igloolik similarly full, the group, left with few options, opted to stay at Al’s B&B.


While mentioning he understands that accommodations in Nunavut hamlets are limited, the commissioner noted Idlout could have consulted his office for advice in the matter before making a claim. 


This is not the first time that the MP has taken steps to remove herself from a perceived conflict of interest. 


In July, Idlout distanced herself from her stake in an Indigenous management consultancy firm by

putting it in a trust

 — a legal arrangement that can hold an asset while a politician is in public office, which prevents them from making income from the asset or selling it. The company, NVision Insight Group, has received $1.5 million in federal contracts since Idlout’s election five years ago.
